lessons.title: The Urban-Rural Continuum in the UK

before.content_html:
A Continuum, Not a Divide

It is tempting to imagine the UK as a sharp split between concrete cities and quiet countryside, but in reality the two blur into each other. Geographers describe the gradual change from inner city through suburb, commuter village, market town and remote farm as the urban-rural continuum. Travel out of central Manchester, for example, and you pass through high-density terraces, suburban semis, commuter villages around Wilmslow, market towns like Macclesfield, and only after an hour reach genuinely remote moorland. The continuum is held together by daily flows: people, goods, services, money and information.

Key Fact

Rural and urban areas of the UK are linked by four main flows: commuting (people travelling to work), shopping (people travelling to retail), services (healthcare, education, leisure) and communications (digital and transport networks).

Population — Where People Live

Around 84 % of the UK population lives in urban areas, but the urban share is highest in the South East, the Midlands conurbations and central Scotland. Rural population concentrates around market towns and along main rail lines — not on isolated farms. The map of UK population is therefore lumpy: dense in cities, thinning rapidly with distance from a large town, and patchy in remote uplands such as Mid-Wales and the Scottish Highlands.

Sphere of Influence

A sphere of influence is the area a settlement serves. Big cities like Birmingham have a national sphere for some services (universities, specialist hospitals) and a local one for others (a corner shop). Each kind of service has a threshold population — the minimum number of users it needs to survive.

A village shop needs a few hundred customers; a GP surgery needs a few thousand; a major hospital needs hundreds of thousands. That is why central Manchester has multiple specialist hospitals, while parts of rural Northumberland are over an hour’s drive from the nearest A&E. People living in remote rural areas often travel further for services, and rural NHS Trusts run extra schemes — mobile clinics, telehealth, community pharmacies — to cover ground that population alone could not justify.

Commuting — The Daily Pulse

More than nine million UK workers commute across the urban-rural boundary every weekday. Cheap fuel and fast trains made it possible to live in a village near Bath and work in central Bristol, or to keep a Lake District home and commute to Carnforth. Counter-urbanisation — people leaving cities for rural living — has been one of the strongest UK trends since the 1990s. Working from home, supercharged by the pandemic, has accelerated it further.

Key Fact

Counter-urbanisation is the move of people from cities to rural areas, often keeping a city job. It is different from suburbanisation, which is movement only to the urban fringe. Eduqas examiners flag this confusion every year.

Retail Links

Shopping is another bridge between rural and urban Britain. Villagers travel into a market town for weekly groceries, into a city for clothes, and increasingly online for everything else. Out-of-town centres such as Cribbs Causeway near Bristol pull customers from a 30 km radius, hollowing out smaller market-town high streets in the process. Online shopping skips the trip entirely — and the parcel still arrives in the most remote village by van.

Rural Change — Two Speeds

UK rural areas are not all going the same way. Accessible rural areas — villages within easy commuting reach of a city — are growing in population, gaining new houses and rising house prices. Remote rural areas, especially uplands and coastal margins, are losing services. Bus routes shrink, schools close, banks vanish, post offices double up as cafes.

Rural deprivation rarely makes headlines because it is dispersed. A 2023 Rural England report found that around 17 % of rural households experience fuel poverty — higher than the urban average — partly because off-grid homes use expensive heating oil. Remote rural wages are about 10 % below the urban average. Without a car, accessing work, shops and healthcare becomes very difficult, and bus services have been cut by over 50 % in some counties since 2010.

Two-Way Influence

The link between rural and urban Britain is not one-way. Rural areas supply cities with food, water, energy and recreation. Reservoirs in the Pennines feed Manchester. Wind farms in mid-Wales send electricity to the National Grid. The North Yorkshire Moors and the South Downs supply weekend escapes for millions of city dwellers. In return, cities send shoppers, second-home buyers, tourists and tax revenue. The continuum is a partnership — sometimes uneven, sometimes contested, but always two-way.
before.exam_tip_html: Eduqas examiners flag two predictable mistakes on this topic. First, students confuse counter-urbanisation with suburbanisation. Make the difference explicit. Second, students describe rural areas as if they all share the same problems. Use the contrast between accessible and remote rural areas, with named examples (Wilmslow vs Mid-Wales, the Cotswolds vs upland Northumberland). For 6-mark questions on links, name a specific city-region (Manchester, Bristol, Newcastle) rather than ‘a UK city’.

lessons.title: Population & Urban Change in the UK

before.content_html:
A Population in Flux

The UK population reached around 67 million in 2021 and is projected to pass 70 million before 2040. Population is changing in three main ways — birth rate has fallen, life expectancy has risen, and net migration is high. The combined effect is an older, larger and more unevenly distributed population than fifty years ago.

Why Birth Rates Have Fallen

In the 1960s, women in England and Wales had on average 2.9 children. By 2021 that figure was 1.6 — below the replacement level of 2.1. Economic factors push couples to delay or limit family size: rising childcare costs, expensive housing and longer time spent in education. Political factors include better access to contraception and women remaining in paid work. Social factors include changing expectations about careers and the choice to have smaller families.

An Ageing Population

An ageing population means that the proportion of people aged 65 and over is rising. By 2021 around 19% of the UK population was aged 65 or above; by 2050 it is forecast to reach 25%. This is the result of better healthcare, falling smoking rates and improved diets that have raised average life expectancy to about 81 years. The Office for National Statistics calls this the ‘greying’ of Britain.

Key Fact

UK population change is driven by three forces — falling birth rates (now around 1.6 children per woman), an ageing population (19% aged 65+ in 2021) and high net migration (around 600,000 in the year to mid-2023).

An older population places pressure on the NHS and adult social care — older patients stay in hospital longer and need more chronic care. Pension spending now accounts for around 10% of all UK government spending. Workforce shortages appear in nursing, teaching and engineering as the over-65 group leaves work faster than school leavers replace them.

There are positives too. Older people contribute through volunteering, unpaid childcare for grandchildren and the ‘silver economy’ of leisure, travel and home-improvement spending. Coastal towns like Eastbourne and Christchurch depend on retirees for local employment.

Migration Into and Within the UK

International migration is the largest single driver of recent UK population growth. Net migration peaked at around 745,000 in 2022 before falling to roughly 600,000 in the year to mid-2023. New arrivals have come from EU countries (especially Poland and Romania between 2004 and 2020), from South Asia and West Africa for work and study, and through humanitarian routes from Ukraine, Hong Kong and Afghanistan.

Internal migration also reshapes the country. London continues to attract young workers in their twenties, while families in their thirties and forties increasingly leave the capital for cheaper towns in the south-east, the Midlands and South Wales — a process called counter-urbanisation. Retirees concentrate in coastal districts like North Devon, parts of East Yorkshire and the Welsh coast.

The Housing Pressure

A larger, older and more dispersed population needs more homes. The 2021 census recorded 24.8 million households — up 1.4 million in a decade — and average household size has fallen as more people live alone in later life. The government estimates that England alone needs around 300,000 new homes every year to meet demand and improve affordability. Actual completions averaged closer to 220,000 in the late 2010s, leaving a persistent shortfall.

Pressure is not spread evenly. Demand is highest in London, the south-east and university cities like Bristol, Manchester and Cardiff. House prices in these areas have risen far faster than wages, and many young adults remain in their parents’ home or rent privately well into their thirties. Rural areas with strong second-home markets, such as parts of Pembrokeshire and the Lake District, have seen local people priced out.

Key Fact

England needs around 300,000 new homes a year to meet demand. In the late 2010s, only about 220,000 were built — a shortfall that pushes up prices, especially in London and university cities.

Around 60% of new homes in England are built on previously developed brownfield land — old industrial sites, former gasworks and disused railway yards. Planning rules favour brownfield because it reuses existing transport links and protects countryside. The remaining 40% takes greenfield sites: edge-of-town fields where building is faster and cheaper. Garden villages such as Northstowe near Cambridge and Bicester in Oxfordshire are large planned greenfield expansions.

Local authorities also approve home extensions and conversions of offices, shops and pubs to flats. Following relaxed permitted-development rules in 2020, an estimated 70,000 office-to-residential conversions were created in England by 2023.

Why It All Connects

The story of UK population change is not three separate trends but one feedback loop. Lower birth rates and longer lives age the workforce; an ageing workforce attracts younger migrants to fill the gaps; new arrivals and family-formers need housing where the jobs are; housing demand reshapes which areas grow and which shrink. Geographers track these flows because every government decision — on immigration rules, on planning permission, on social care funding — ripples through all four trends at once.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK population is rising past 67 million but birth rates have fallen to 1.6 children per woman; growth is driven mainly by net migration.
  • An ageing population (19% aged 65+) puts pressure on the NHS, social care and pensions but supports a growing ‘silver economy’.
  • England needs around 300,000 new homes a year — a target rarely hit — with greatest demand in London, the south-east and university cities.

knowledge_checks.q: Which figure is closest to the UK birth rate in 2021?
Roughly how many new homes does England need each year to meet demand?
An _____ population means that the proportion of people aged 65 and over is rising.
The movement of people out of a city to live in smaller towns or rural areas is called _____.
Match each cause of UK population change to its main effect:
right: Smaller average family size, household size falls
Larger over-65 group; pension and care costs rise
Population growth concentrated in cities and university towns

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the UK's birth rate in 2021?
A) Above the European average
B) Around 1.6 children per woman, below replacement level
C) Roughly equal to the death rate
D) Higher than in the 1960s
practice_questions.marks: B) Around 1.6 children per woman, below replacement level [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two consequences of an ageing UK population.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each consequence described, up to two:
• Increased pressure on the NHS and adult social care because older people need more chronic and end-of-life care.
• Higher government spending on the state pension (around 10% of all government spending).
• Workforce shortages in nursing, teaching and engineering as people retire faster than they are replaced.
• A growing 'silver economy' as retirees spend on leisure, travel and home improvements.
• Concentration of older residents in coastal towns such as Eastbourne, supporting local services.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why net migration into the UK is currently high.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three linked reasons developed with cause-effect chains and named examples (e.g. EU work migration after 2004, humanitarian routes from Ukraine and Hong Kong, international students from South Asia).
Secure: Two clear reasons explained with cause-effect, at least one named example.
Developing: Two reasons stated with limited explanation, or one developed reason.
Emerging: One simple reason; little or no explanation.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the housing pressures faced by London with those faced by a rural area such as Pembrokeshire.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparison using linking words (whereas, in contrast, similarly). Both areas covered with specific detail — London's price-to-wage gap and high demand from young workers contrasted with Pembrokeshire's second-home market and locals priced out.
Secure: Clear comparison with linking words and relevant detail for both places.
Developing: Some comparison; tends to describe each place separately rather than link them.
Emerging: One place described; little or no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a UK example, explain how migration has changed the population of a city or town. Refer to specific places, numbers or features in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A named UK place (e.g. Boston in Lincolnshire, Leicester, Cardiff) with specific evidence — figures, source country, time period — and a clear chain explaining at least two consequences (e.g. demand for housing, pressure on schools, economic contribution, cultural change).
Secure: A named place with relevant detail and at least two explained consequences.
Developing: A named place with limited detail; one consequence explained.
Emerging: General reference to migration with no place-specific detail.
[6 marks — locational detail is essential]

practice_questions.text: 'Building 300,000 new homes a year is the only realistic answer to the UK's housing crisis.' Evaluate this statement. Reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The shortfall between need (~300,000) and completions (~220,000) is the direct cause of unaffordable prices, especially in London and the south-east.
• A larger supply would slow price rises and let young adults move out of the family home.
• Brownfield development can deliver new homes without significant countryside loss.

Arguments against:
• The target alone does not control where homes are built; demand is concentrated and rural areas with second-home pressure may not benefit.
• Greenfield expansion meets resistance from local communities and damages habitats.
• Housing supply is one driver; affordability also depends on interest rates, wages and immigration policy.
• The shortage is partly a distribution problem — empty homes in northern towns sit alongside crowded southern markets.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with both sides developed using named places, weighted judgement and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger than the other; conclusion stated but limited justification.
Emerging: Simple points; little judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

before.exam_tip_html: Eduqas examiners often ask candidates to use specific places. For 6-mark questions on UK retail change, name a town — Stockton-on-Tees, the Metro Centre, Bluewater — and lock in two facts (vacancy rate, parking spaces, year). For 4-mark ‘Compare’ questions, weave together out-of-town and high-street streams using linking words. For 8-mark evaluations, do not just list costs and benefits — weigh them and reach a clear judgement (which group of shoppers benefits most or least?).
before.content_html:
A Retail Revolution

Until the 1980s most UK shopping happened on the high street. By 2024 fewer than 35% of retail sales happened there. Three forces have rewritten where, when and how people buy — economic, cultural and technological. Understanding the change matters because the high street is not just an economic space; it is also where communities meet.

The Rise of Out-of-Town Centres

Out-of-town retail parks took off in the 1980s. The Metro Centre near Gateshead opened in 1986 with 2 million sq ft of floor space and around 10,000 free parking spaces. Bluewater (Kent, 1999) and Cribbs Causeway (Bristol, 1998) followed. By 2020 there were more than 1,500 retail parks in the UK.

Why have they grown? Economic factors: lower land costs on the urban edge let supermarkets and chain stores build bigger units. Cultural factors: rising car ownership (around 80% of UK households own a car) made parking the most important convenience. Technological factors: large warehouses with refrigeration and stock-control software allow one site to stock far more lines than a high-street shop. Customers can park, eat at a chain restaurant, watch a film and complete all their shopping in one trip.

Key Fact

Out-of-town retail has grown because land is cheaper, car ownership is high (around 80% of households) and large warehouses can stock more lines. The Metro Centre alone has 2 million sq ft of floor space and 10,000 parking spaces.

Benefits: Free parking and longer opening hours suit working families. Lower rents allow shops to keep prices down. Out-of-town parks employ thousands — the Metro Centre supports about 9,000 jobs. They concentrate retail traffic on a few well-built roads, easing town-centre congestion.

Costs: Heavy car use raises CO2 emissions and air pollution; few customers arrive on foot or by bike. Independent high-street shops lose footfall and close. Land that was once farmland or scrub is permanently sealed under tarmac. People without cars (older residents, students, low-income households) struggle to reach out-of-town parks at all.

The Internet Shopping Surge

If the 1980s were the decade of the retail park, the 2010s were the decade of the screen. Internet shopping rose from around 5% of UK retail sales in 2008 to a peak of 38% during the 2020 lockdown, settling at around 26% in 2024. Amazon UK alone employs more than 75,000 people and operates over 30 fulfilment centres.

Drivers were technological: faster broadband, smartphones, contactless payment and same-day delivery networks; economic: price-comparison sites force prices down; and cultural: younger shoppers expect to research, review and buy from a phone. The shift was accelerated dramatically by Covid-19 lockdowns from March 2020 onwards, when non-essential shops were forced to close.

High Street Change — A UK Case Study: Stockton-on-Tees

Stockton High Street — one of the widest in England — tells the story of UK high-street change in miniature. By 2018 the vacancy rate was around 19% (the UK average is closer to 14%). Department-store chain Debenhams closed its Stockton branch in 2021. The Castlegate shopping centre, built in the 1970s, was demolished in 2023.

Stockton-on-Tees Borough Council’s response shows how UK high streets are being reinvented. The £40 million Globe theatre reopened in 2021 as a 3,000-seat live-music venue. The Castlegate site is being replaced by a riverside urban park and new homes. Independent traders have moved into the Shambles, a converted Victorian market hall. Shopping is no longer the only purpose of the high street — leisure, food, services and housing are filling the floor space chain shops have left behind.

Key Fact

Stockton-on-Tees responded to a 19% high-street vacancy rate by reopening the Globe theatre (3,000 seats, 2021), demolishing the 1970s Castlegate centre for an urban park, and bringing independent traders into the Shambles market hall.

Many UK high streets share Stockton’s pattern. Department stores have collapsed: BHS in 2016, House of Fraser stores throughout the 2010s, Wilko in 2023. Banks have closed an estimated 6,000 branches since 2015 as customers move to mobile banking. The gaps are filling with charity shops (now around 11,000 across the UK), barbers, nail bars, vape shops, gyms and chain coffee outlets.

Government has responded with the Future High Streets Fund and Town Deals, distributing more than £1 billion to over 100 towns since 2019. Conversions of upper-floor offices to flats are common. The trend is from ‘shopping streets’ back to ‘mixed-use streets’ that combine retail, leisure, services and homes.

An Evolving Identity

UK retail has not died — it has split. Convenience and bulk shopping have moved out of town or online. Experience and social shopping have stayed central, but in a slimmer, more leisure-focused high street. The towns that adapt fastest will be those that treat their high street as a meeting place first and a shopping destination second.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes an out-of-town retail park?
A) A traditional shopping street in the centre of a town
B) A large retail centre on the edge of a town with extensive free parking
C) A small parade of shops next to a housing estate
D) A weekly outdoor market in a market square
practice_questions.marks: B) A large retail centre on the edge of a town with extensive free parking [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why UK internet shopping has grown rapidly since 2010.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each reason described, up to two:
• Faster broadband and smartphone use let customers research, compare and buy from anywhere.
• Same-day and next-day delivery networks remove the need to visit shops.
• Covid-19 lockdowns from March 2020 forced non-essential shops to close, accelerating online use.
• Price-comparison sites push prices down and make online cheaper than high-street equivalents.
• Younger shoppers expect a digital-first experience.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why some UK high streets have lost shoppers in the last twenty years.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three reasons explained with cause-effect chains and named context (e.g. out-of-town parks like the Metro Centre offer free parking, internet shopping at 26% of sales pulls trade online, department-store collapses such as Debenhams leave gaps).
Secure: Two clear reasons explained.
Developing: Two reasons stated with limited explanation.
Emerging: One reason with little explanation.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare shopping at an out-of-town retail park with shopping on a traditional UK high street.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparison using linking words (whereas, in contrast, similarly). Both settings covered with specific detail — out-of-town free parking and longer hours, contrasted with high-street pedestrian access, mix of independents and lower car emissions.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail for both.
Developing: Some comparison; describes each setting separately.
Emerging: One setting described; little or no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a UK case study, explain how a town or city has tried to revive its high street.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A named UK case study (e.g. Stockton-on-Tees) with specific evidence — 19% vacancy rate, Globe theatre reopened 2021 (3,000 seats), Castlegate centre demolished 2023, Shambles for independents — linked to at least two reasons the actions help (footfall, mixed use, reduced reliance on chain retail).
Secure: Named place with detail and at least two explained changes.
Developing: Some place-specific detail; one change explained.
Emerging: General reference to high-street change with no named place.
[6 marks — locational detail is essential]

practice_questions.text: 'The growth of internet shopping has done more harm than good to UK towns and cities.' Evaluate this statement. Reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (more harm):
• Online sales reaching 26% of UK retail in 2024 has cut high-street footfall, contributing to chain failures (Debenhams, BHS, Wilko).
• Empty units lower the appeal and tax base of towns; vacancy rates around 14% nationally.
• Delivery vans add traffic and emissions in residential streets.

Arguments against (more good):
• Customers in rural areas with poor transport now have access to the same range as cities.
• Lower prices benefit lower-income households.
• High streets are reinventing themselves as leisure and mixed-use spaces (Stockton's Globe theatre, Castlegate park) — a positive shift, not a death.
• Online retailers create jobs (Amazon UK over 75,000) and new fulfilment centres support post-industrial regions.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with both sides developed using named places, weighted judgement and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; conclusion stated but limited justification.
Emerging: Simple points; little judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]

before.content_html:
A World of Cities

In 2008, for the first time in human history, more than half of the world’s population lived in towns and cities. By 2024 the figure passed 57%. The number of global cities — New York, London, Tokyo, Shanghai, Mumbai, Lagos — has grown alongside this shift. Their distribution has changed too: in 1950 most megacities were in high-income countries, while today most are in Asia and Africa.

Comparing London and Mumbai

For Eduqas you must study one city in a high-income country (HIC) and one in a low- or newly-industrialised country (LIC/NIC). London (UK, HIC) and Mumbai (India, NIC) are used here. Both are global cities — financial centres, transport hubs and media powerhouses — but the way each grows and the problems each faces look very different.

Why London Grew

London’s population reached around 9.0 million in 2024, up from 7.0 million in 2000. Growth comes mainly from international migration rather than natural increase — over 40% of Londoners were born outside the UK. The city pulls migrants because of pull factors: financial-sector jobs in the City and Canary Wharf, world-leading universities, and the English language.

Internal migration matters too. Young UK adults move to London for graduate jobs (push factor: limited career options in some northern towns). Some Londoners then move out again in their thirties when they start families — a flow tied to high housing costs.

Why Mumbai Grew

Mumbai’s population is around 21 million, having grown from 12 million in 1990. Most growth comes from internal rural-to-urban migration, with around 1,000 people arriving every day. Push factors in rural Maharashtra and Bihar: small landholdings, drought, low rural wages and limited rural healthcare. Pull factors in Mumbai: the docks, Bollywood (the world’s largest film industry by volume), the textile industry, and IT and finance jobs in the Bandra-Kurla Complex.

Mumbai is also connected internationally — over 50 million passengers passed through Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport in 2019, and the city is India’s busiest port. Migration from across South Asia has made Mumbai one of the most linguistically diverse cities in the world.

Key Fact

London’s population reached around 9.0 million in 2024, growing mainly through international migration. Mumbai’s population is around 21 million, growing through internal rural-to-urban migration with about 1,000 arrivals each day.

Ways of Life in London

London is one of the most ethnically diverse cities in Europe — the 2021 census found over 300 languages spoken. The wealthiest areas (Kensington and Chelsea, Westminster) sit minutes from some of the most deprived (parts of Tower Hamlets and Newham). Average life expectancy in Kensington is about 84 years; in some neighbourhoods of Tower Hamlets it is closer to 78. Housing affordability is the biggest day-to-day pressure: average house prices passed £530,000 in 2024.

Ways of Life in Mumbai

Mumbai shows extreme contrasts on a single street. Antilia, a private 27-storey skyscraper home, sits on the same skyline as Dharavi — a 2 sq km area where roughly 700,000 people live, work and trade. Dharavi is part of the informal economy: pottery, leather, recycling and food workshops generate around US$1 billion of trade a year, but most workers have no contracts, no sick pay and no formal protection.

Around 60% of Mumbai’s working population are estimated to be in informal jobs — street vendors, dabbawalas (lunchbox couriers), domestic workers, recyclers in Dharavi. The informal economy provides essential goods and services cheaply and creates work for new arrivals who would otherwise be unemployed.

The downside: workers earn little, conditions are dangerous (Dharavi’s recycling sheds use chemicals without ventilation), tax revenue is missed, and women in informal work are especially exposed to harassment. Schemes such as the Self Employed Women’s Association (SEWA) try to give informal workers some collective bargaining power.

Current Urban Challenges

London: housing affordability is the headline crisis — over 165,000 people in the capital are in temporary accommodation. Air pollution has been linked to early deaths in poorer neighbourhoods, prompting the Ultra Low Emission Zone in 2019. Reducing deprivation requires regeneration that does not simply price out long-term residents.

Mumbai: providing decent housing for its huge informal sector is the biggest challenge. The Dharavi Redevelopment Project, restarted in 2022 with the Adani Group, plans to rehouse residents in modern flats and convert the rest into commercial space. Critics worry that the relocations will break the network of micro-businesses that gives Dharavi its income. Air pollution and monsoon flooding are also worsening as the city expands.

Key Fact

London faces housing affordability and air pollution — over 165,000 in temporary accommodation, with the Ultra Low Emission Zone since 2019. Mumbai faces housing 700,000 people in Dharavi alone, addressed by the restarted Dharavi Redevelopment Project (2022).

Connected to the World

Both cities are anchors in the network of globalisation. London is a centre of finance (the City), media (BBC, Reuters) and aviation (Heathrow handled around 79 million passengers in 2023). Mumbai is the headquarters of the Reserve Bank of India, the centre of Bollywood, and a key port for Indian Ocean trade. Both attract migrants, both export culture, and both shape the global economy through finance and media.
before.exam_tip_html: Eduqas examiner reports stress that ‘a city in Africa’ or ‘a city in Asia’ loses marks at 6 and 8 mark tariffs. Always name your two cities — London and Mumbai — and lock in numbers (9.0m / 21m population, 700,000 in Dharavi, 165,000 in temporary housing, 1,000 daily arrivals). For 4-mark ‘Compare’ questions, use linking words to weave the two cities together. For 8-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions, judge whether challenges are mostly the same or mostly different and justify with evidence.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • London (HIC, around 9.0 million people) grows mainly through international migration; Mumbai (NIC, around 21 million) grows through rural-to-urban migration with about 1,000 arrivals daily.
  • Both cities show extreme inequality — Kensington next to Tower Hamlets, Antilia next to Dharavi — but Mumbai’s informal economy employs around 60% of its workforce.
  • Globalisation links both cities through finance, media and transport — Heathrow with 79 million passengers, Mumbai port handling India’s busiest trade.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the informal economy?
A) Trade carried out only between large multinational companies
B) Small-scale, unregistered businesses that are not regulated or taxed
C) Government-run shops and services in a city centre
D) Online shopping completed through registered platforms
practice_questions.marks: B) Small-scale, unregistered businesses that are not regulated or taxed [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which Mumbai is connected to the rest of the world.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each connection described, up to two:
• Bollywood is the world's largest film industry by volume, exporting Indian culture worldwide.
• Mumbai is India's busiest port, handling much of the country's international trade.
• Chhatrapati Shivaji International Airport handled over 50 million passengers in 2019.
• Mumbai is the headquarters of the Reserve Bank of India and a major financial centre for South Asia.
• Migration from across South Asia and the Indian diaspora connects the city worldwide.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why London continues to grow in population.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Three reasons explained with cause-effect chains and named detail (e.g. international migration drawn by financial-sector jobs in the City; world-leading universities pulling students; English-language advantage; over 40% of Londoners born outside the UK).
Secure: Two reasons clearly explained.
Developing: Two reasons stated with limited explanation.
Emerging: One reason with little explanation.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare the way of life in London with the way of life in Mumbai.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparison using linking words. Both cities covered with named detail (Kensington vs Tower Hamlets, Antilia vs Dharavi; average house prices £530,000 vs Dharavi 700,000 residents in 2 sq km).
Secure: Both cities named with relevant detail; clear comparison.
Developing: Two places mentioned but described separately.
Emerging: One city described; little or no comparison.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Using a named LIC or NIC city, explain how rural-to-urban migration has shaped its growth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A named LIC/NIC city (e.g. Mumbai) with specific evidence — population growth from 12m in 1990 to 21m today, around 1,000 arrivals daily, push factors (drought, small landholdings) and pull factors (docks, Bollywood, IT) — linked to at least two consequences (Dharavi housing pressure, informal economy, Bandra-Kurla Complex jobs).
Secure: Named city with detail and at least two explained consequences.
Developing: Some place-specific detail; one consequence explained.
Emerging: General reference to migration with no place-specific detail.
[6 marks — locational detail is essential]

practice_questions.text: 'The challenges faced by global cities in HICs and LICs/NICs are essentially the same.' Evaluate this statement using London and Mumbai. Reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (similar challenges):
• Both cities face extreme inequality between richest and poorest neighbourhoods (Kensington vs Tower Hamlets in London; Antilia vs Dharavi in Mumbai).
• Both must provide affordable housing under heavy population pressure.
• Both face air pollution and traffic congestion.

Arguments against (different challenges):
• Mumbai's main housing problem is informal settlement (700,000 in Dharavi alone) — London's is unaffordable formal housing (165,000 in temporary accommodation).
• Around 60% of Mumbai's workers are in the informal economy with no protection; London's labour market is overwhelmingly formal.
• Mumbai's population growth is driven by internal rural-to-urban migration; London's by international migration.
• Climate vulnerability differs — Mumbai faces monsoon flooding on a scale London does not.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with both sides developed using named places and figures, weighted judgement and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides argued with relevant evidence and a clear conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; conclusion stated but limited justification.
Emerging: Simple points; little judgement.
[8 marks + 4 SPaG]
